title: Latent Context Language Models: Compressing the Prompt, Not the Cache
hook: Instead of shrinking the KV cache, compress the prompt itself: a small encoder folds a long context into a few latent embeddings that a bigger decoder reads — letting agents skim and expand on demand.
key_points: Long-context inference is bottlenecked by the KV cache, which grows with context length; KV-cache compression either hurts quality or is too slow.
LCLMs instead use a 0.6B encoder to map a long token sequence into a much shorter sequence of latent embeddings consumed by a 4B decoder.
Trained from scratch via architecture search, then continually pre-trained on 350B+ tokens per model at 1:4, 1:8, and 1:16 compression ratios.
Improves the accuracy–speed–memory Pareto frontier and acts as a backbone for long-horizon agents that skim compressed context and expand relevant parts on demand.
content_html: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by memory: the KV cache grows with the context length. Existing fixes that compress the KV cache fall short — they either degrade quality substantially or take a lot of time and compute to compress a single long prompt, and many require the input to fit the model's context window and don't play well with production inference engines.
extra_html:
The idea

The authors revisit encoder–decoder compression: map a long token sequence into a shorter sequence of latent embeddings that a decoder consumes. Earlier attempts weren't competitive, so the team first ran an architecture search, pre-training many variants from scratch to learn how best to design and train such compressors. Guided by that, they continually pre-trained a family of 0.6B-encoder, 4B-decoder models on over 350B tokens each, at compression ratios of 1:4, 1:8, and 1:16. The result is Latent Context Language Models (LCLMs).

Why it matters

LCLMs push the Pareto frontier across general-task performance, compression speed, and peak memory at once — the three axes earlier methods had to trade off. The authors also show LCLMs make efficient backbones for long-horizon agents: the agent skims a compressed long context and adaptively expands the segments it actually needs, rather than paying full memory cost up front.

related.title: Ring Attention for Near-Infinite Context
related.hook: Spread one long sequence across many devices and compute attention blockwise - the context length you can handle grows with the number of devices, all with exact attention and no extra overhead.

related.title: Extending Context Windows via Positional Interpolation
related.hook: Don't extrapolate to positions the model never saw - squeeze the position indices back inside the trained range, and a short fine-tune stretches the context window many times over.

related.title: Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer
related.hook: Most tokens only need to look at their neighbors, so swap full attention for a sliding window plus a few global tokens and the cost goes from quadratic to linear in sequence length.

flashcards.prompt: How do Latent Context Language Models cut long-context memory cost?
flashcards.back_html: A small encoder compresses the input token sequence into a much shorter sequence of latent embeddings (e.g. 1:8) that a larger decoder consumes — compressing the prompt itself rather than the KV cache.

flashcards.prompt: Why did the authors revisit encoder–decoder compression instead of compressing the KV cache?

choices.text: KV-cache methods either degrade quality or are slow, often need the input to fit the context window, and don't fit production engines
Encoder–decoder compression requires no training at all
KV-cache compression only works for image inputs

flashcards.explanation_html: Existing KV-cache compression falls short on the accuracy–efficiency frontier and is hard to deploy; the paper revisits encoder–decoder compression to close that gap.

flashcards.prompt: What advantage do LCLMs give long-horizon agents?
flashcards.back_html: They let an agent skim a compressed long context cheaply and adaptively expand the relevant segments on demand, instead of holding the full context in memory.
